newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Premier wants agreed bid for Discovery.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Premier wants agreed bid for Discovery.

text.p: Premier Oil Plc said it would meet executives of takeover target Discovery Petroleum NL on Thursday in an attempt to reach terms on an agreed offer.
"An agreed bid is always preferable. It obviously makes the process a lot smoother," Premier's general manager of international and new business, Stephen Lowden, told Reuters.

Lowden said Premier may consider increasing its A$91.2 million bid beyond the current 70 cents a share if the Australian petroleum producer and explorer could prove that its assets were worth more than Premier now believed.
Discovery has rejected Premier's hostile bid, calling it too low.

The local company, with key assets in Indonesia and Australia, has won the support of share market speculators who have pushed the stock to 80 cents in the belief that this is the latest rationalisation move in the Australian petroleum sector.
Oil Search Ltd, which is based in Papua New Guinea, paid 75 cents per share for a 10.1 percent stake in Discovery on September 27, describing it as a strategic purchase.
It said Discovery was a well-managed firm with exploration and development potential, particularly in Southeast Asia.
Lowden said he was not surprised that another company would move onto Discovery's share register during the takeover.
"I suppose I wasn't surprised to see somebody else emerge, but what was a surprise was to see it being Oil Search because I don't see Oil Search having that much to gain from Discovery.
"I can see that they want to diversify out of PNG but I wouldn't have thought it would be a very good or very efficient way to do that."
Premier said it believed the valuation of Discovery at between 77 cents and 95 cents per share was partly based on an overly optimistic view of Discovery's exploration potential.
Lowden said Premier, one of the United Kingdom's independent producers and explorers, would meet Discovery chairman Peter Jones and managing director Eric Streitberg in Sydney on Thursday afternoon.
"I think you could say Premier may consider a higher bid if the value (of Discovery's assets) can be clearly demonstrated," he said of the upcoming meeting.
Lowden said the rise in Discovery's share price to 80 cents was partly due to generous bids for local firms, citing the agreed takeover of Command Petroleum Holdings NL by Cairn Energy Plc.
"That price reflects as much the industry high as it does reflect any perceived future bid that Premier may or may not make."

Premier announced the bid on September 23, saying Discovery lacked the financial clout to develop its attractive assets and noting the offer price was higher than Discovery had traded in the past two years.

Lowden said Premier had a "very good handle on the core value" of Discovery but was concerned about the value placed on its exploration assets, particularly in the Perth and Carnarvon Basins of Western Australia.
About 70 percent of Discovery's income is derived from its 18.75 percent stake in Indonesia's Kakap gas field, which is operated by Clyde Petroleum Plc.

Mobil Corp began the latest round of takeovers in February 1996 when it bid A$1.78 billion for oil producer and explorer Ampolex Ltd. The bid is now nearing completion following a deal struck last month with noteholders.
Clyde followed soon after with a successful bid for onshore oil and gas producer Crusader Ltd. Analysts said foreign companies had recognised that local assets were undervalued.
